overview: The two thyroid hormones differ mainly in iodine content, potency, and how much of each the thyroid actually secretes.
genZNote: T4: made in bulk, needs converting. T3: the more powerful, ready-to-use form.

aspects.label: Relative Potency
aspects.valueA: About 3-5 times more biologically potent than T4.
aspects.valueB: Less potent per molecule, but secreted in much larger quantities.

aspects.label: Amount Secreted by Thyroid
aspects.valueA: Secreted in smaller amounts directly by the thyroid.
aspects.valueB: The major hormone secreted directly by the thyroid gland (about 90% of output).

aspects.label: Conversion
aspects.valueA: Mostly produced by peripheral conversion of T4 in tissues like the liver.
aspects.valueB: Converted to the more active T3 in peripheral tissues as needed.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Most T3 in the body doesn't come directly from the thyroid — it's produced by converting T4 in peripheral tissues.
overlay.memoryTrick: T3 = 3 iodines, more potent. T4 = 4 iodines, the main one secreted.
overlay.commonMisconception: T4 is not the 'inactive' hormone — it is biologically active on its own, just less potent than T3, and serves as a stable circulating reservoir.
